claims.text: Superconductivity in the proposed class of uncharacterized high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by disorder-mediated modulation of electron–phonon coupling.
A controlled mixture of heavy and lighter transition metals softens phonon modes.
The proposed starting material is a fully disordered, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
Heavy-transition-metal concentration will be systematically varied while phase and crystal structure are held constant.
Chemical disorder softens local vibrational modes.
Atomic mass mismatch among the constituent elements softens local vibrational modes.
Chemical disorder and atomic size or mass differences produce local lattice strain.
Local lattice strain associated with chemical disorder and constituent mismatch produces soft phonon modes.
Soft phonon modes enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling increases the superconducting pairing interaction.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling can modify the superconducting transition temperature.
A higher proportion of heavy transition metals promotes softer phonon modes.
Increasing the heavy-transition-metal proportion will increase the electron–phonon coupling constant relative to the baseline.
Increasing the heavy-transition-metal proportion will increase Tc relative to the baseline.
The balanced-composition baseline exhibits a measurable superconducting transition under the synthesis conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
Different mechanisms may dominate in multiphase or partly ordered alloys.
Magnetic interactions or additional scattering mechanisms may alter the effect of heavy-element concentration on electron–phonon coupling and Tc.
Failure of increased heavy-element content to enhance both electron–phonon coupling and Tc relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
